title: Patio Orientation
body: The patio house wall faces 230° (southwest) . This is the toughest orientation for Houston gardening. Implications and mitigations for Outdoor Garden Layout and Garden Monitor. What 230° Means - No morning sun — the house blocks east light from the patio. - Full-blast afternoon sun — from roughly noon through sunset. The hottest, most intense window of the day in Houston. - Wall radiates absorbed heat — the house wall acts as a thermal mass, soaking sun all afternoon and re-emitting heat onto the plants long after the sun moves off. - Microclimate is hotter than ambient — soil surface in the raised bed could hit 130°F+ in July/August without mulch. Even ambient air against the wall sits 5–10°F above the local forecast. Per-Crop Heat Tolerance | Crop | Tolerance | What happens at this orientation | |---|---|---| | 🍅 Tomato (Beefsteak) | Drops flowers and stops setting fruit above 95°F. | Spring harvest May–June, then production pause June–September until nights cool. Fall production resumes late September. | | 🌶️ Bell Pepper, Jalapeño | More heat-tolerant than tomato. | Produce through summer with watering discipline. Jalapeños actually thrive. | | 🍉 Watermelon | Loves heat IF watered consistently. | Will keep producing all summer; needs daily watering. | | 🌽 Corn | Moderate. | Has the wind/grass area; gets more balanced sun than the wall plants. | | 💜 Lavender | Mediterranean — wants heat + dry. | Thrives. The hot wall actually suits it. | | 🌿 Spearmint | Wilts in afternoon sun. | Already showing stress — needs partial shade or relocation. | | 🍋 Lime tree | Heat-loving. | Thrives. | | 🥗 Lettuce / Cilantro | Bolts above 80°F. | Don't even try outdoors here past April. Indoor / hydroponic only. | Mitigations 1. Straw mulch everywhere (already applied) Already in place across raised bed, corn containers, herbs. Drops surface soil temp 15–20°F. Single highest-impact thing in Houston gardening. Pull mulch ~1" away from each stem to prevent rot. 2. Morning watering only Plants need to be hydrated before the afternoon assault hits. Evening watering = wet foliage overnight + Houston humidity → fungal pressure (powdery mildew, black spot). Water at the base, never on leaves. See Watering Guide for per-plant schedules. 3. Shade cloth (deploy late May) Get 40–50% shade cloth (white or aluminet/reflective silver). Drape over the raised bed during peak afternoon hours (~1 PM to 5 PM). Drops effective temp 10–15°F — the difference between tomatoes producing and shutting down. Don't go higher than 50% shade — plants still need light to fruit. Don't deploy before late May either — early-season plants want all the sun they can get to establish strong root systems. See Shade Strategy for the PVC frame design. 4. Plant placement within the bed - Tomatoes at the east end of the raised bed — they catch the least direct wall-radiated heat (the east end is furthest from peak afternoon sun angle on a 230° wall). - Peppers/jalapeños in the middle — they handle the hottest zone best. - Onions tucked between — short, doesn't compete for vertical space, cool roots from neighbor shade. 5. Spearmint relocation Mint is the plant most stressed by this orientation. Options: - Move to a partial-shade spot if any exists (e.g., east side of the house if accessible). - Upsize the pot and water more frequently. - Accept the seasonal hit — mint often goes "summer dormant" in Houston and rebounds in fall. 6. Container-level heat management Dark plastic containers (corn, watermelon) absorb a lot of solar. Mulch on top of the soil drops surface temps; consider also wrapping the outside of the container in light-colored fabric or shade cloth for the worst heat weeks if leaves start curling. 7. Future: temperature-driven automation Once Garden Monitor is wired up, Arduino Nicla Sense Env + DHT22 sensors at each zone log to InfluxDB on the Raspberry Pi 5. Rules to deploy: - Delay watering past 6 PM if ambient 100°F (avoid evening leaf-wetness). - Auto-trigger sha

title: Shade Strategy
body: Shade cloth design for the raised bed in Outdoor Garden Layout — protection from late-May through mid-September Houston afternoon heat. Critical given the Patio Orientation. Why You Need It Tomatoes drop flowers + stop setting fruit above 95°F. The southwest-facing patio wall pushes the raised bed's effective temperature 5–15°F above ambient most afternoons June–September. Shade cloth restores tomato production through summer. Without shade cloth on a 230°-facing bed, expect: - Tomato production pause: June through September. - Pepper / jalapeño: still produce but stressed. - Soil surface temps at the bed: 130°F+ in peak afternoon (mulch keeps the root zone livable, but leaves get cooked). With 40–50% shade cloth deployed afternoon hours (1–5 PM): - Effective temp drops 10–15°F. - Tomato production continues into July. - Less leaf burn across all crops. Specs | Item | Spec | Why | |---|---|---| | Shade rating | 40–50% | Balance — enough shade to drop temp, enough light to fruit. 50% blocks too much light; <40% doesn't drop temp enough. | | Color | White or aluminet (reflective silver) | Reflects heat instead of absorbing. Avoid black — gets hot itself. | | Frame material | 1" PVC pipe + tee fittings | Cheap, lightweight, reusable, no glue (so it disassembles seasonally). | | Vertical pipe height | ~5 ft | Above the bed wall, allows 6 ft tomato growth underneath. | | Crossbar length | ~8 ft (matches bed length) | Spans the long edge of the raised bed. | Frame Design Verticals: Two 5-ft 1" PVC pipes at the back corners of the raised bed (against the wall side). Crossbar: One 8-ft 1" PVC pipe across the top, joined to the verticals with tee fittings (no glue). Anchoring: Either (a) clamp the verticals to the bed walls with large hose clamps or U-bolts, or (b) sink them 8–10" into the soil inside the bed at each end — bed wall provides lateral support. Cloth attachment: Eye hooks on the house wall above the window for the rear of the cloth. Binder clips or zip ties to the front of the crossbar. Cloth drapes from wall down over the crossbar and angles forward like an awning. Bottom open: Don't enclose — air must flow underneath, otherwise it becomes an oven. Materials List | Item | Source | Approx. cost | |---|---|---| | 1" PVC pipe (10 ft) × 2 | Home Depot / Lowe's | ~$8–10 | | 1" PVC tee fittings × 2 | Home Depot / Lowe's | ~$3 | | 1" PVC end caps × 2 (optional) | Home Depot / Lowe's | ~$2 | | Hose clamps (large) × 4 OR U-bolts × 4 | Home Depot / Lowe's | ~$5 | | Eye hooks × 2 | Home Depot / Lowe's | ~$2 | | 6 × 8 ft (or 6 × 10 ft) shade cloth panel, 40–50%, white/aluminet | Amazon (search "shade cloth 50% white 6x8") | ~$15–25 | | Binder clips (jumbo, 8-pack) | Already on hand or ~$3 | | | Zip ties (variety pack) | Already on hand or ~$3 | | Total: ~$35–45. Timing | Date | Action | |---|---| | Early–Mid May | Don't deploy yet. Plants want full sun while establishing. | | Late May / Early June | Deploy when daily highs consistently hit 95°F+ . | | June – September | Keep deployed during peak afternoon (~1–5 PM). Can leave up 24/7 — Houston nights stay warm enough that morning sun still gets through the cloth's diffused light. | | Late September | Remove when daily highs drop below 90°F. Tomatoes resume fruit set. | Daily Operation (Manual) Two options: 1. Deploy once, leave up all summer. Simplest. The 40–50% rating still allows enough light through morning + diffused light, and the angle puts most blockage on afternoon sun. 2. Deploy/retract daily. Higher labor but maximum morning sun. Pull cloth back at 5–6 PM, redeploy at noon. Cloth folds into a small bundle; takes 30 seconds. For most of summer, option 1 is the right tradeoff. Why NOT a Pop-Up Canopy A pop-up shade canopy (tailgate-style) would be easier to deploy, BUT: - Houston thunderstorms blow them away (lost canopies = ~$60 each + plant damage if it falls). - Not anchored to the structure. - Hard to angle correctly for a SW-facing wall. The PVC frame is sturdier, ancho

title: Outdoor Garden Layout
body: Patio garden design for Garden Monitor — raised bed, corn containers, watermelon trellis, herb stand, lime tree, and potato tower. Houston stone patio, southwest-facing house wall. Site - Stone patio against the house wall. Wall faces 230° (southwest) — see Patio Orientation for the heat-management implications. - Hose spigot accessible at one end of the patio (future drip irrigation tap point). - Raised bed sits on stone, not soil — drainage layer matters. Layout Map Raised Bed (8' × 2' × 16–18" deep, galvanized steel) Already built and placed against the house wall. Mulched with straw, ready for transplants. Plant placements (best 2 of each variety, transplanted at 4–6 true leaves): - 2 × Tomato (Beefsteak) — 24" apart, with cage or stake each. Place at the east end where they'll catch the least afternoon-wall heat. - 2 × Bell Pepper (CA Wonder) — 18" apart, middle. - 2 × Jalapeño (Gigante) — 18" apart, middle near peppers (same family, similar needs). - 8 × Onion (Evergreen Bunching) — tucked between the larger plants (tiny footprint). - Basil — between tomatoes (companion plant; supposedly improves flavor + repels some pests). - ~~Broccoli~~ — Houston summer kills heading. Save seedlings for fall replant. Planting hole protocol: 1 Tbsp Trifecta Myco Supreme into each hole. Set root ball on top, backfill. Don't combine with Miracle-Gro synthetic fertilizer (kills the fungi). Use compost tea or fish emulsion instead. Why this layout: - 2 ft wide max — reachable from the front (back is against the wall). - 12" minimum depth required for tomato/pepper roots; 16–18" is even better in Houston summer when shallow soil cooks. - Landscape fabric on the bottom of the bed before filling — prevents soil washing through onto the patio while still allowing drainage. Soil Calculation 16 cubic feet needed for a 2' × 8' × 12" bed. Add 15% for settling = ~18 cu ft. | Bag size | bags | |---|---| | 2 cu ft (standard) | 8–10 | | 1.5 cu ft | 11–12 | Cost-saving mix recipe (instead of all premium potting): - 40% topsoil (cheap, ~$3/bag) - 40% compost (~$5/bag) - 20% perlite (~$5/bag) → Total ~$40–60 vs $70–130 for all-premium. Existing Miracle-Gro can fill in as part of the compost portion (just not in spots that will get Myco Supreme later). Corn Containers Two large circular planters (~18–20" diameter) sitting on grass off the patio. - 5 stalks per container in a cross pattern — 1 in center, 4 around at ~8" from center. - 10 plants total across both pots — tight for wind pollination but workable since the containers are touching each other. - When tassels appear, shake them gently each morning to drop pollen onto silks below. - Mulch with 2–3 inches of straw , leaving a 1" gap around each stalk (no stem rot). Watermelon One vine only , trained vertically up a trellis against the house wall. In its own 15–20 gallon container (or 5-gallon bucket minimum) — NOT in the raised bed. Why not the raised bed: watermelon is one of the heaviest feeders + drinkers in gardening. Roots spread 2–3 ft wide; would invade tomato/pepper space within weeks and stress everything. Vertical training: trellis leaning against the wall behind the pot. Vine climbs; fruit hangs in mesh slings. Yield: 2–3 melons (5–8 lbs each) — plenty for one household. Existing Plants (Stay in Place) - Herb stand (wicker frame): lavender box, citronella pot, spearmint pot. - Potato tower (clothes hamper, layered soil/hay system) — already producing top growth and side-hole sprouts. Add another soil/hay layer on top as plants grow taller (more tubers per buried stem section). - Lime tree (kaffir/citrus) — healthy, may flower this season. Eventually upgrade to a 15–20 gallon pot. - Carrot — 5-gallon bucket with drilled drain holes (carrots need 12+ inches of depth). - Oregano + Rosemary — terracotta pots once nursery-started seedlings are ready. title: Indoor Nursery
body: Status snapshot of the indoor seed-starting nursery for Garden Monitor. Seeds planted 2026-04-14 , four trays of 12 cells each on the Nursery System Design. Garage location, Houston. Shelf-by-Shelf Layout | Shelf | Tray | Contents | |---|---|---| | Shelf 4 (top) | Big container (12 cells) + egg carton | 2 bell pepper, 2 jalapeño, 2 tomato, 4 onion · egg carton: assorted peppers/tomatoes/jalapeños in eggshell halves | | Shelf 3 | 12-cell tray | Bell pepper, tomato, onion (4 each) | | Shelf 2 left | 12-cell tray | Corn (Golden Bantam), broccoli (Waltham), carrot (Scarlet Nantes) | | Shelf 2 right | 12-cell tray | Oregano, rosemary, watermelon | | Shelf 1 (bottom) | 12-cell tray | Three lettuce varieties: Buttercrunch Butterhead, Ruby Red, Black Seeded Simpson | Layout is intentional: heat rises inside the PVC cover, so warm-season crops (peppers, tomatoes, jalapeños) sit on the upper shelves and lettuce stays at the bottom where it's coolest. Natural temperature gradient = no second heat mat needed. 📸 Photo placeholder — overall shelf view, day 7 (2026-04-21) Germination Status (Day 5–10) | Status | Items | |---|---| | ✅ Growing well | Corn (star — 4–5" → 8–10" by day 10), watermelon, broccoli, onion, single tomato | | 🟡 Just starting | A few lettuce sprouts (Black Seeded Simpson, Ruby Red), bell pepper sprout | | 🔴 No signs after 10+ days | Top shelf big container + egg carton (likely heat-killed — see below) | | ⏳ Normal — still in window | Carrot (10–14 days), oregano (7–14), rosemary (14–21) | ⚠️ Heat Issue — Resolved The garage greenhouse hit 37°C / 98.6°F at the top shelf during peak afternoon — caused by Houston ambient + grow lights + sealed PVC cover. Lettuce went thermodormant; top-shelf seeds likely got cooked. Temperature timeline: | Reading | Conditions | What it means | |---|---|---| | 37.0°C / 98.6°F | Top shelf, afternoon, cover closed | Too hot for everything — even peppers stress at 95°F+ | | 33.3°C / 91.9°F | Bottom shelf, afternoon, covers off | Still too hot for lettuce (thermodormancy 75°F) | | 25.2°C / 77.4°F | Bottom shelf, 7:20 AM, covers off, 70% RH | Workable for most crops; borderline for lettuce | Mitigations applied: - PVC cover fully off during the day , only on at night if garage drops below 65°F. - Box fan pointed at shelves for airflow — drops effective temp 5–10°F. - Hygrometer moved to bottom shelf to track lettuce zone. - Top-shelf big container declared dead — focus shifted to the strong Shelf 3 tray. 📸 Photo placeholder — hygrometer reading (37°C / 98.6°F), then 25.2°C morning reading Eggshell Planters Note Many top-shelf cells use eggshell halves with cracked tops sitting in a cardboard egg carton. The shells are essentially mini sealed pots — moisture stays in much longer than bare cardboard. Adjustments: - Reduce misting to once daily (vs twice for plastic cells). - 1–2 teaspoons max per shell per misting — eggshells don't drain. - Poke a pin hole in the bottom of each shell for drainage and to enable bottom-watering from the carton. - Bonus at transplant: crack the shell more around the sides and plant the whole thing . Eggshell decomposes and releases calcium carbonate → prevents tomato blossom-end rot. Watering Schedule See Watering Guide for the full per-shelf rules. Quick version: cells should feel like a wrung-out sponge (damp throughout, never wet). Water daily on Shelf 4 (driest), every 1–2 days on Shelves 1–3, twice daily on the egg carton. Myco Supreme Don't apply yet. Mycorrhizal fungi need active root contact to colonize. Hold until transplant day for tomatoes, peppers, jalapeños, watermelon, corn — sprinkle 1 Tbsp into each planting hole. Outdoor lavender/citronella/spearmint can get a dose now (already-established root systems). See Transplant Timeline for dates. What's Working / Not Working Working: - Tier strategy — heat-loving crops up top, lettuce on bottom = natural temp zoning. - Shelf 3 tray (peppers/tomatoes/onions) is the breakout success. - Eggshell technique

title: Transplant Timeline
body: Per-plant readiness criteria and target dates for moving seedlings from the Indoor Nursery to the Outdoor Garden Layout. Updated as the Garden Monitor nursery progresses. The Rule A seedling is ready to transplant when it has 4–6 true leaves AND the stem is thick enough to support upright growth. Cell-bound (roots circling the bottom) means overdue . Current Status — Day 12 since 2026-04-14 planting | Plant | Source tray | Days to ready | Target date | Status | |---|---|---|---|---| | Corn (Golden Bantam) | Shelf 2 left | OVERDUE — roots cell-bound | Today (transplant immediately) | 🚨 | | Watermelon | Shelf 2 right | ~3–7 days | Within 10 days | 🟡 — leggy, needs stem mounding now | | Tomato (Beefsteak) | Shelf 3 | 14–21 days | ~2 weeks | ⏳ — wait for 4–6 true leaves | | Bell Pepper | Shelf 3 | 14–21 days | ~2 weeks | ⏳ | | Jalapeño Gigante | Shelf 3 (+ duplicates lost on Shelf 4) | 14–21 days | ~2 weeks | ⏳ | | Onion (Evergreen Bunching) | Shelf 3 | 7–14 days | 1–2 weeks | 🟡 | | Broccoli | Shelf 2 left | N/A — Houston summer kills heading | Hold for fall replant in August | ⏸️ | | Carrot | Shelf 2 left | N/A — taproot doesn't transplant | Direct sow outdoors instead | ⏸️ | | Oregano | Shelf 2 right | 21–28 days | ~3–4 weeks | ⏳ | | Rosemary | Shelf 2 right | 28–35 days | ~4–5 weeks | ⏳ — slowest grower | | Lettuce (3 varieties) | Shelf 1 | N/A this season — bolts in heat | Hydroponics or fall replant | ⏸️ | Watermelon — Stem Mounding Fix The watermelon stems got leggy (too thin to support seed leaves; some fell over). Cause: light wasn't close enough during the high-heat days. Fix: - Mound soil up around fallen stems , burying partway up to just below the seed leaves. - Watermelon (like tomatoes) grows roots from buried stem — this actually helps long-term root mass. - Lower the grow light to 2–3 inches above the tallest plant on that shelf. - Real solution: get them outdoors. Sun is 5–10× more intense than grow lights and builds stronger stems naturally. Hardening-Off Checklist Don't take seedlings from indoor nursery to direct outdoor sun in one move — they'll sunburn and shock. Instead, harden off over 5–7 days : - [ ] Day 1: 1 hour outdoors in shade. - [ ] Day 2: 2 hours outdoors, partial shade. - [ ] Day 3: 3–4 hours outdoors, partial sun (morning OK). - [ ] Day 4: Half day outdoors, including some direct sun. - [ ] Day 5: Full day outdoors, dappled sun. Bring in for night. - [ ] Day 6: Full day + leave out overnight if temps stay above 60°F. - [ ] Day 7: Transplant. ⚠️ Skip hardening only if seedlings have already been exposed to high heat in the nursery (Houston garage heat counts) AND the transplant date has cooler weather forecast. Transplant-Day Protocol (per plant) 1. Water the seedling tray an hour before — easier extraction, less root damage. 2. Dig the planting hole to the depth of the cell + 1" extra. For tomatoes/peppers/jalapeños: dig deeper and bury part of the stem (they grow extra roots from buried stem = stronger plant). 3. Drop in 1 Tbsp Trifecta Myco Supreme at the bottom of the hole. 4. Pop the cell out gently. If roots are circling the bottom, loosen them with fingers or a chopstick. 5. Set the root ball on top of the Myco — roots in direct contact with the inoculant. 6. Backfill with soil , firming around the base. Don't pack too hard. 7. Water deeply — soak until water runs out the bottom. 8. Mulch with 2–3" straw, keeping a 1" gap around the stem. 9. For tomatoes, peppers, jalapeños: stake or cage immediately. Don't wait until they need it — driving stakes later damages roots. 10. For corn: plant in the cross pattern (1 center + 4 around at 8" from center) per Outdoor Garden Layout. Two containers touching each other for cross-pollination. 11. For watermelon: single vine in the 15–20 gal container by the trellis. Train the main vine up the trellis as it grows (loose ties). 12. title: Watering Guide
body: Per-plant watering schedules for the Garden Monitor indoor nursery and outdoor garden. Houston (Zone 9a, southwest-facing patio). The Universal Rule Soil should feel like a wrung-out sponge — damp throughout but never sitting in water. Stick your finger ¼" into the soil. If it feels dry, water. If it's still moist, leave it alone. Indoor Nursery — Seedling Stage | Tray / Location | Frequency | Method | Volume | |---|---|---|---| | Plastic cells (Shelves 1–3) | Every 1–2 days | Spray bottle / gentle mist | 1–2 Tbsp per cell, until surface evenly damp | | Big container (Shelf 4) | Every 1–2 days, water when top ¼" dry | Mist or gentle pour | More volume, deeper soak | | Egg carton (Shelf 4) — eggshell halves | Once daily (sealed eggshells retain moisture) | Mist | 1–2 tsp max per shell — easy to overwater | | Cardboard egg carton without shells | Twice daily (cardboard wicks fast) | Mist | Just enough to dampen cardboard visibly | When True Leaves Appear (~Week 2–3) Switch to bottom watering : - Pour water into the black catch tray. - Let cells wick moisture from below for ~20 min. - Dump any standing water afterward. - Encourages roots to grow downward + prevents damping-off (fungal seedling killer). Don't Do - ❌ Pour water directly onto seeds or tiny sprouts (dislodges them, compacts soil). - ❌ Leave standing water in catch trays 30 min (root rot, damping-off). - ❌ Mist top of eggshells if water pools and doesn't absorb in 1 minute (overwatering — shells don't drain). - ✅ Tip: Pin a tiny hole in the bottom of each eggshell for drainage. Heat Adjustments Warm shelves (3–4) dry faster than the cool bottom (lettuce). PVC cover helps retain humidity. Crack open the cover for 30 min daily for air circulation — prevents mold without dropping humidity too far. Outdoor — Per Plant Raised Bed (Pre-Transplant) - Frequency: Every 2–3 days while empty (just keep soil moist for transplant readiness). - Mulch covers everything; pull aside at planting spots when transplant day comes. Tomatoes (Raised Bed) — Once Transplanted - Frequency: Deep soak every 2–3 days; daily during establishment week. - Method: At the base, never on leaves (Houston humidity + wet foliage = fungal disaster). - Time: Morning only. Evening watering leaves wet leaves overnight. - Volume: Until water runs out the bottom of the bed. Shallow watering = shallow roots = stressed plants in summer. Peppers + Jalapeños (Raised Bed) - Same as tomatoes; slightly more drought-tolerant. Every 3 days fine in mild weather; daily in 95°F+ stretches. Onions (Raised Bed) - 1–2× per week. Don't overwater — onions rot in soggy soil. Surface dries between waterings is fine. Basil (Raised Bed) - More frequent than tomatoes; basil wilts visibly when thirsty. Every 1–2 days. Recovers fast after a soak. Corn (Circular Containers) - Establishment week (post-transplant): Deep soak every morning. Until water runs out the bottom drain holes. - Established (~week 2+): Stick finger 2" into soil under the straw. If dry at that depth, water. Daily in May/June heat. - At tasseling: Don't let it dry out — pollination is moisture-sensitive. - Time: Morning only. Watermelon (Container with Trellis) - Establishment week: Deep daily watering. - Established: Stick finger 2" deep under straw. Likely daily, sometimes twice daily above 95°F. Watermelon is 92% water by weight — needs constant supply for fruit. - At fruit set: Keep watering consistent . Erratic watering causes cracking + hollow heart. - One week before harvest: Reduce to every other day. Slight stress concentrates sugars = sweeter fruit. - Method: Base only, slow trickle under the straw. - Time: Morning only. - Harvest signs: Tendril nearest the fruit turns brown; belly spot turns from white to yellow. Lavender Box (Existing Herb Stand) - Frequency: Once a week max once established. Drier the better. - Method: Base only — wet foliage in Houston humidity = black leaves and death. - Cooldown: Minimum 4–5 days between waterings — enforced in Outdo

title: Nursery System Design
body: Indoor seed-starting nursery for Garden Monitor — drip irrigation, sensor wiring, camera, and tier strategy for the SOLIGT 5-tier greenhouse on the Raspberry Pi 5 / older Pi node. Hardware (Owned + Purchased) - SOLIGT 5-tier greenhouse — 63" tall, includes lights, timer, hygrometer, PVC cover. All-in-one nursery shelf. - Trifecta Myco Supreme — mycorrhizal fungi for transplant. - Miracle-Gro potting soil — but don't combine with Myco Supreme (high phosphorus kills the beneficial fungi). - 2 × Capacitive Soil Moisture Sensor (Gikfun, already on hand). Components to Add (~$50–70) | Item | Search term | Approx. cost | |---|---|---| | 12V DC submersible pump (240 L/H, 3m head) | SIPYTOPF DC 12V submersible pump 240L/H 3M head | ~$7 | | 12V 2A DC power adapter | | ~$9 | | Adjustable drip emitters (50-pack) | MIXC 50pcs drip emitters fan stake 1/4 inch | ~$8 | | ADS1115 16-bit I2C ADC | HiLetgo ADS1115 16 bit I2C | ~$6 | | 5-pack Gikfun capacitive moisture sensors | (same brand as already owned) | ~$8 | | 4-channel relay module | | ~$6 | | DHT22 temp/humidity sensor | | ~$6 | | Jumper wires kit | | ~$7 | | Pi Camera Module (OV5647 IR-Cut, 5 MP) | Aokin Raspberry Pi camera IR-Cut OV5647 5MP | ~$12 | Total nursery system investment: ~$310–340 all-in including the SOLIGT shelf. 1. Pump Sizing The shelf is 63" tall (~5.3 ft). Pump must push water from a floor reservoir up to the top tier. - Head height is the key spec — get a pump rated for 6–10 ft of head for comfortable margin. - Flow rate matters less here — drip, not flood. 80–120 GPH at 5 ft head is plenty. - 12V DC submersible is preferred over USB — switchable via relay from the nursery Pi's GPIO for Garden Monitor automation integration. 2. Plumbing Layout - ½" main tubing (50 ft kit) runs vertically up the back of the shelf. - ½" elbow fittings (La Farah) turn the line horizontal at each tier. - ½"-to-¼" barbed tees (Kalolary) tap off at each tray position. - ¼" distribution tubing (Hourleey 50 ft) goes from each tee to a drip stake. - Adjustable drip emitters (~$8 / 50-pack) at the end of each ¼" line — dial flow per tray. Lettuce needs less than peppers. - End cap the ½" main line at the top (or fold-and-clamp). - PVC liners that come with the shelf catch drainage on each tier; can drip back down to the reservoir (closed loop) or into separate trays. 3. Moisture Sensor Architecture - Older Raspberry Pis have no analog input — capacitive sensors are analog, so we need an ADS1115 16-bit ADC over I2C . - ADS1115 gives 4 analog channels — enough for one sensor per tier on tiers 1–4. Tier 5 either shares with tier 4 or daisy-chains a second ADS1115. - Each sensor pushes into the soil of a representative tray on its tier. - Pi reads moisture every 30 seconds via I2C, publishes to MQTT topics like garden/nursery/tier1/moisture . - Hub evaluates threshold; pump relay fires for 10–15 seconds (calibrate from there). - Phase 2 upgrade: Add a small solenoid valve on each tier's ½" branch line, individually relay-controlled. Then we can water tier 3 (peppers) without watering tier 1 (lettuce that's already moist). 4. Camera Integration - Pi Camera Module (OV5647) mounted on the top tier looking down — captures tiers 1–3 from above. - Connects via CSI ribbon cable directly to the nursery Pi. - Schedule: capture every 4–6 hours. Generate timelapse via raspistill / libcamera . - One camera can't see all 5 tiers usefully — for full coverage, add a second on the bottom tier looking up, or build a motorized vertical slide rail (fun future project with a stepper + Arduino). - The Arduino Nicla Vision is better used outdoors where its edge ML and standalone WiFi shine. 5. Tier Layout Strategy Heat rises naturally inside the PVC enclosure — exploit this for free temperature zoning instead of buying a second heat mat: | Tier | Temp zone | Best for | |---|---|---| | Top (5/4) | Warmest (75–85°F) | Tomatoes, peppers, jalapeños, basil, watermelon | | Middle (3/2) | Moderate | Onions, oregano, rosemary

title: Houston Planting Calendar
body: Zone 9a (Houston, TX) seed-by-seed planting decisions for the Garden Monitor system. Last frost mid-February; March is the most valuable planting window of the year. Plant RIGHT NOW (Direct Seed Outdoors) - Okra (Clemson Spineless) — Houston's #1 summer crop. 1" deep, 12–18" apart. Soak seeds overnight first. Harvest in 55–65 days, produces straight through October. - Cucumber — 1" deep, 36" apart (sprawls). Trellis or cage saves space. Inconsistent moisture causes bitter fruit. Harvest 50–70 days. - Corn (Sweet) — Direct seed when soil temp hits 60°F. Plant in 4×4 blocks minimum (wind-pollinated). 1" deep, 10–12" apart. Not practical container-only. - Watermelon / Cantaloupe — Hill mounds, 2–3 seeds per hill, 1" deep. 6–8 ft per vine sprawl. Compact varieties for containers. 80–90 days to fruit. - Basil (Genovese & Lemon) — Barely cover seeds (need light to germinate). 12" apart. Pinch flower buds for season-long leaf production. Start Seeds Indoors NOW (Transplant in 3–4 Weeks) - Tomato — Heat mat 70–80°F, ¼" deep. 6–8 weeks to transplant size. Mid-May transplant is workable but tight before summer heat. For spring tomatoes from store transplants instead, plant the seeds for fall (transplant in July). - Pepper / Jalapeño Gigante — Same as tomato. 75–85°F soil. More heat-tolerant than tomatoes; produces well into Houston fall. - Rosemary — Slow germinator (14–21 days). 70°F soil. Perennial in Houston once established. Excellent drainage required — hates wet feet. Plant Now But Manage Expectations - Lettuce (Little Gem & Gourmet Blend) — Tail end of season. Will bolt mid-April–May. Better as a hydroponics crop or fall replant in September. Indoor in cool zone for now. - Cilantro — Bolts fast at 80°F+. Maybe 3–4 weeks of harvest. Let some flower for coriander seed. Save for fall. - Carrot — Direct sow OK now, but they prefer cooler soil. Deep container with loose mix, barely below surface, 10–14 days to germinate. Save for Fall (August–September Start) - Broccoli — Cool-season. Spring start = May transplant = bolts before heading. Start indoors August, transplant September. - Onion (Sweet Spanish) — Onion seed needs October–January start in Houston. Buy onion sets (small bulbs) for spring. Already Planted / Perennials - Spearmint and Lavender — Established outdoors. Apply Myco Supreme to root zone now. Mycorrhizal fungi dramatically improve nutrient/water uptake (especially for lavender). My Recommended Allocation - Outdoor containers: Okra, both basils, cucumber. - Indoor nursery: Tomato, pepper, jalapeño, rosemary, lettuce, cilantro. - Hydroponics (future): Lettuce (Gourmet Blend). - Potato tower: Need actual seed potatoes (not from packet) — get from nursery. - Hold for fall: Broccoli, onion seed, carrot, second lettuce/cilantro round. - Space-dependent: Corn (4×4 minimum), watermelon (6+ ft sprawl), cantaloupe — patio-only is a tough grow. --- Links: Garden Monitor · Outdoor Watering System · Indoor Nursery · Outdoor Garden Layout #garden-monitor #planting #houston #zone-9a #seasonal

title: Wiring Guide
body: Step-by-step beginner wiring guide for the Garden Monitor project. ⚠️ Always wire with the Arduino unplugged from USB/power . --- What You Need for This Step | Item | Qty | Notes | |------|-----|-------| | Arduino Mega 2560 | 1 | The big blue board | | Gikfun Capacitive Soil Moisture Sensor v1.2 | 2 | The black PCB sticks | | Jumper wires (female-to-male) | 6 | 3 wires per sensor | | USB Type-B cable | 1 | To connect Mega to your PC (and later to Pi 5) | | A cup of water + dry soil | — | For calibration testing | --- Understanding the Sensor Your Gikfun capacitive soil moisture sensor v1.2 has 3 wires coming from a connector: | Wire Color | Label on PCB | What It Does | |-----------|-------------|-------------| | Red | VCC | Power (3.3V or 5V) | | Black | GND | Ground | | Yellow | AOUT | Analog signal output (the moisture reading) | The sensor outputs a voltage on the yellow wire that changes based on moisture: - Dry air/soil → higher number (around 500–600) - Wet soil/water → lower number (around 200–300) 💡 Capacitive sensors are better than the cheap metal-prong ones because they don't corrode over time in wet soil. --- Understanding the Arduino Mega Pins Looking at the Arduino Mega with the USB port facing LEFT: We need: - A0 — Analog pin for Sensor 1 (Lavender zone) - A1 — Analog pin for Sensor 2 (Potato tower zone) - 5V — Power for both sensors - GND — Ground for both sensors --- Step-by-Step Wiring Sensor 1 — Lavender Zone (Zone 2) | Sensor Wire | → | Arduino Mega Pin | How to Find It | |------------|---|-----------------|----------------| | Red (VCC) | → | 5V | Bottom-left power cluster, labeled "5V" | | Black (GND) | → | GND | Right next to 5V, labeled "GND" | | Yellow (AOUT) | → | A0 | Bottom edge, first analog pin, labeled "A0" | Sensor 2 — Potato Tower (Zone 4) | Sensor Wire | → | Arduino Mega Pin | How to Find It | |------------|---|-----------------|----------------| | Red (VCC) | → | 5V | Same 5V pin (can share with Sensor 1) | | Black (GND) | → | GND | Same GND pin (can share with Sensor 1) | | Yellow (AOUT) | → | A1 | Bottom edge, second analog pin, labeled "A1" | 💡 Sharing power pins is fine. Both sensors draw very little current. You can plug both red wires into the same 5V pin and both black wires into the same GND pin. If it's physically difficult, the Mega has multiple GND pins — use any of them. --- Wiring Diagram (Visual) ![Soil moisture sensor wiring to Arduino Mega 2560](/ assets/wiring-soil-sensors.svg) Wiring Diagram (Text Version) --- After Wiring — Quick Checklist - [ ] Red wires go to 5V (NOT 3.3V — these sensors work better at 5V with the Mega) - [ ] Black wires go to GND - [ ] Yellow wire from Sensor 1 goes to A0 - [ ] Yellow wire from Sensor 2 goes to A1 - [ ] No wires are touching each other where they shouldn't - [ ] USB cable is plugged into the Mega's USB-B port - [ ] The other end of the USB cable goes to your PC (for now) or Pi 5 (later) --- Next Step → Go to Arduino Setup Guide to install the Arduino IDE and upload the sensor reading code. --- Links: Garden Monitor · Outdoor Watering System · Capacitive Soil Moisture Sensor · Arduino Mega · Arduino Setup Guide #garden-monitor #wiring #beginner

body: Step-by-step guide to install the Arduino IDE, upload code, and read soil moisture sensors. Part of the Garden Monitor project. --- Overview — What We're Building By the end of this guide, your Arduino Mega will: 1. Read 2 soil moisture sensors every 5 seconds 2. Print the readings to the Serial Monitor (so you can see them on your PC) 3. Send JSON-formatted data over USB serial (so the Pi 5 can read them later) 4. Blink the onboard LED when it takes a reading (so you know it's working) --- Part 1: Install Arduino IDE Step 1 — Download 1. Go to https://www.arduino.cc/en/software 2. Download Arduino IDE 2.x for Windows 3. Run the installer, accept defaults, click through Step 2 — First Launch 1. Open Arduino IDE 2. It will download some initial packages — let it finish 3. You should see a blank sketch with setup() and loop() Step 3 — Connect Your Arduino Mega 1. Plug the USB-B cable into the Mega and into your PC 2. In Arduino IDE, look at the top toolbar — you should see a dropdown that says something like: - Arduino Mega or Mega 2560 on COM3 (the COM number may vary) 3. If it says "No board selected": - Click the dropdown → Select board → Search for "Mega" - Select Arduino Mega or Mega 2560 - Select the COM port that appeared when you plugged in 💡 Not seeing a COM port? You may need the CH340 USB driver if your Mega is a clone. Search "CH340 driver download" and install it. --- Part 2: Upload the Sensor Reading Code Step 4 — Create a New Sketch 1. In Arduino IDE: File → New Sketch 2. Delete everything in the editor 3. Copy and paste the entire code below (also saved at Software/Arduino/garden monitor sensors.ino in this vault) Here is the complete code: Step 5 — Upload the Code 1. Make sure your Mega is selected in the board dropdown (top toolbar) 2. Click the → (Upload) button (right arrow icon in the top-left) 3. You'll see: - "Compiling sketch..." (wait 10–20 seconds) - "Uploading..." (a few seconds) - "Done uploading." ← success! ⚠️ If you get an error, check: Is the correct board selected? Is the correct COM port selected? Is the USB cable a data cable (not charge-only)? Step 6 — Open the Serial Monitor 1. Click Tools → Serial Monitor (or the magnifying glass icon top-right) 2. Make sure the baud rate dropdown at the bottom says 9600 3. You should see output like: 🎉 If you see JSON lines appearing every 5 seconds, your wiring is correct and the code is working! --- Part 3: Calibrate Your Sensors The raw readings will only mean something useful after you calibrate them with YOUR soil. Step 7 — Dry Air Baseline 1. Hold both sensors in the open air (not touching anything) 2. Note the raw values — they should be around 550–600 3. Write down the number: DRY AIR VALUE = Step 8 — Water Baseline 1. Put both sensors in a cup of water (only the black PCB part — keep the connector and wires DRY) 2. Note the raw values — they should drop to around 200–280 3. Write down the number: WATER VALUE = Step 9 — Update Calibration in Code 1. In the Arduino code, find these lines near the top: 2. Replace the numbers with YOUR measured values 3. Re-upload the code (click Upload again) Step 10 — Soil Test 1. Stick Sensor 1 into the lavender pot soil 2. Stick Sensor 2 into the potato tower soil 3. Watch the readings — the percentage should now show a meaningful 0–100% moisture level 4. Water the soil a bit and watch the numbers change — they should go UP toward 100% 5. Let it dry and watch them go DOWN toward 0% --- Part 4: Understanding the Output Each line the Mega sends looks like this: | Field | Meaning | |-------|---------| | lavender raw | Raw analog reading (0–1023) from the lavender sensor | | lavender pct | Moisture percentage (0% dry → 100% wet) | | potato raw | Raw analog reading from the potato sensor | | potato pct | Moisture percentage | | uptime sec | How many seconds the Mega has been running | --- Troubleshooting | Problem | Fix | |---------|-----| | All readings are 0 | Check wires — yellow wire probably not connected to A0/A

title: Outdoor Watering System
body: Detailed system design for automated watering of 4 plant zones on the south side of the house in Houston, TX. Part of the Garden Monitor project · See also System Architecture --- Site Overview - Location: South side of house, Houston TX (USDA Zone 9a) - Sun exposure: ~6–7 hours direct sun per day - Climate: Hot, humid subtropical — summers routinely 95–100°F with high humidity - Key challenge: Houston heat + humidity means plants can cook if overwatered (wet foliage + heat = fungal death), but potted plants dry out fast in direct sun --- The 4 Zones Zone 1 — Spearmint (1 plant, single pot) Watering profile: HIGH moisture demand - Mint needs consistently moist soil — it wilts visibly when thirsty but rebounds fast - In Houston summer heat, potted mint may need watering daily or every other day - In scorching Texas summers, mint often goes into "hibernation" and looks rough — it'll come back when temps cool - Water at the base, keep foliage dry to prevent fungal issues (rust is common on mint in Houston) - Let the top inch dry between waterings, but don't let it go bone dry Sensor strategy: 1 × Capacitive Soil Moisture Sensor Threshold: Water when reading drops below "moist soil" calibration (~350–400 range, TBD after calibration) Watering duration: Short burst — 10–15 seconds of pump flow, then wait and re-check Special notes: - Mulch the pot to reduce evaporation - Consider afternoon shade if plant struggles in peak summer - Spearmint in a pot in Houston = daily water monitoring is critical --- Zone 2 — Lavender (3 plants, rectangle pot) Watering profile: LOW moisture demand — the opposite of mint - Lavender is Mediterranean — it wants to be dry between waterings - In Houston's humidity, lavender is more likely to die from overwatering than underwatering - Water deeply but infrequently — once a week at most when established, maybe less - The saying from Texas lavender growers: "If you think it needs water, wait until tomorrow" - Water at the base ONLY — wet foliage + Houston humidity = black leaves and death - Mulch with gravel or expanded shale (NOT organic mulch) to keep lower foliage dry and reflect heat - Excellent drainage is absolutely critical — the rectangle pot needs drainage holes and fast-draining soil mix (sand/perlite heavy) Sensor strategy: 1 × Capacitive Soil Moisture Sensor (shared across the rectangle pot) Threshold: Water ONLY when reading drops well into "dry soil" range (~450–500+, TBD) Watering duration: Deep soak — 20–30 seconds of pump flow, then don't water again for days Cooldown period: Minimum 4–5 days between waterings , enforced in firmware Special notes: - Best lavender varieties for Houston: Sweet Lavender, Fern Leaf, or French/Spanish types - Don't expect lavender to last more than 2–3 years in Houston — it's not their climate - Don't over-fertilize — lavender likes lean soil - ⚠️ This zone needs the OPPOSITE logic from mint — the system must prevent accidental overwatering --- Zone 3 — Citronella (1 plant, single pot) Watering profile: MODERATE moisture demand - Citronella (scented geranium / Pelargonium citrosum) is drought-tolerant but appreciates regular moisture - Water when the top inch of soil is dry — roughly every 2–3 days in Houston summer - Good drainage is essential — citronella gets root rot from standing water - Can handle Houston's heat and humidity reasonably well - Benefits from afternoon shade in peak summer - Fertilize container-grown citronella biweekly during growing season Sensor strategy: Share sensor data with Zone 1 OR dedicate a sensor if budget allows (we only have 2 sensors currently — see [Sensor Allocation](#sensor-allocation) below) Threshold: Water when reading drops to "moderately dry" range (~400–440, TBD) Watering duration: Medium — 12–18 seconds of pump flow Special notes: - Citronella is toxic to pets — placement matters if dogs/cats are around - Pinch tips regularly for bushier, more fragrant growth - Bring indoors before first frost (typically late Novembe

body: How all the hardware and software connects in Garden Monitor. --- Architecture Documents - Outdoor Watering System — Detailed 4-zone irrigation design with per-plant watering profiles, sensor allocation, firmware logic, physical layout, and Houston-specific considerations - This page — Overall system connectivity and communication --- High-Level Overview --- Communication Protocols | From | To | Protocol | Data | |------|----|----------|------| | Soil Moisture Sensors | Arduino Mega | Analog wire | Voltage (moisture) | | Arduino Nicla Sense Env | Arduino Mega | I2C | Temp, humidity, gas | | Arduino Mega | Raspberry Pi 5 | USB Serial (UART) | JSON sensor packets | | Arduino Nicla Vision | Raspberry Pi 5 | WiFi (HTTP/MQTT) | Images, health alerts | | Raspberry Pi 5 | Arduino Mega | USB Serial | Watering commands per zone | | Raspberry Pi 5 | ESP Display 5in | WiFi (MQTT) | Dashboard data | | Raspberry Pi 5 | Phone/PC | WiFi (HTTP) | Web dashboard | --- Data Flow 1. Sense — Soil moisture per zone (analog), temp/humidity/gas (I2C), soil temp (future DS18B20) 2. Collect — Arduino Mega polls sensors every 5 min, packages as JSON, sends over serial 3. Process — Pi 5 receives data, stores in DB, evaluates per-zone thresholds 4. Act — Per-zone watering decisions: open correct solenoid valve + run pump for zone-specific duration 5. Display — Dashboard updates on ESP Display 5in and/or web UI with per-zone status 6.
